video_title: All About The Fed, The Economy & Inflation
gist: In a September 22 webinar, Ed Yardeni argues the FOMC under Kevin Worsh has entered a rate-hiking cycle (reversing 2024-2025 cuts) because Middle East-driven oil prices threaten stickier inflation, while his 'FIMO vs FOMO' framework shows fabulous earnings momentum outrunning valuation expansion, keeping stocks reasonably priced. He keeps his S&P 500 targets of 8,400 (pushed to mid-2026) and 10,000 by decade's end intact under a 'Roaring 2020s' thesis.

themes.theme: Fed Enters a Hiking Cycle Under Kevin Worsh

insights.claim: The FOMC unanimously raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points at its September 2026 meeting, a decision Yardeni reads as the start of a hiking cycle rather than a one-off move.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors should price in a genuinely hawkish Fed path, not a single symbolic hike, when setting duration and equity valuation assumptions.

insights.claim: Yardeni believes the Fed's three 2025 rate cuts (following a 100-basis-point cut in 2024) were unjustified 'insurance' cuts, since the economy stayed resilient, inflation remained sticky near 3%, and labor market data such as 4.1% unemployment (full employment) and declining initial jobless claims show the labor market never actually weakened.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If the labor-market rationale for prior cuts was weak, the bar for the Fed to cut again is high, supporting a higher-for-longer rate regime that investors should not fade.

insights.claim: Fed Chair Kevin Worsh has repeatedly emphasized at the June and July meetings, at Jackson Hole, and again in September that the Fed has failed to hit its inflation target for over five years running.
insights.speaker: Kevin Worsh (Fed Chair), relayed by Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A Fed chair repeatedly stressing a multi-year inflation-target miss signals sustained hawkish messaging, reducing the odds of near-term rate relief.
insights.quote: the Fed hasn't gotten inflation right for over five years

insights.claim: Based on the FOMC's summary of economic projections, the market has concluded the September hike is not a one-and-done move, and expects at least one or two more rate hikes.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Positioning for further hikes argues for caution on rate-sensitive equity valuations (high-multiple growth) and duration risk in bond portfolios.

insights.claim: Trump and Treasury Secretary Bessant have been publicly praising Kevin Worsh rather than pressuring the Fed to cut, because Yardeni thinks they have concluded that cutting rates now would send bond yields soaring rather than help the administration.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Reduced political interference in Fed policy lowers the risk of a politically forced premature cut that could spook the long end of the bond market.
insights.quote: Bessant and Trump uh both keep saying Wors is a great guy. He's the right guy for the job.

insights.claim: The Fed's meeting-by-meeting path shows a deliberate hawkish drift: in June it held rates unanimously after oil prices had already fallen; in July three members dissented in favor of a hike but Worsh did not join them; at Jackson Hole talk turned more hawkish as a Middle East memorandum of understanding collapsed and oil rose back toward $110; and in September the committee hiked unanimously.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Tracking the sequence of dissents and rhetoric versus the oil price gives investors an early read on when the committee is likely to convert hawkish talk into an actual hike.

themes.theme: Oil and Middle East Geopolitics as the Inflation Wildcard

insights.claim: Houthi advances toward the Red Sea shipping strait and reported strikes on Saudi Arabia drove renewed volatility in oil markets, yet oil prices actually fell over the following couple of days because ample global oil supply is still finding its way to market.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Geopolitical oil-supply shocks are being absorbed by ample global supply, which argues against assuming every Middle East flare-up translates into a durable oil price spike.

insights.claim: The key swing variable for Fed policy is whether oil stabilizes near $100 a barrel, which would produce stickier core inflation via CPI, core PCE, and core PPI (requiring more Fed hikes), or falls back toward $80, which would ease inflation pressure.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Investors should watch the $80-$100 oil range as a near-real-time proxy for how many additional rate hikes the Fed is likely to deliver.

insights.claim: US breakeven inflation rates declined after the Fed's September rate hike, which Yardeni interprets as the Fed regaining credibility with the bond market.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Falling breakevens after a hawkish move is a signal that markets believe the Fed's inflation-fighting resolve, supportive of the 10-year yield holding near 5% rather than spiking further.

themes.theme: FIMO vs FOMO: Earnings Outrunning Valuation

insights.claim: Analysts' 2027 S&P 500 earnings-per-share estimate currently stands at about $419, and Yardeni expects it to rise to roughly $425 by year end.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: This forward EPS number, combined with whatever multiple the market assigns, is the direct input into Yardeni's year-end S&P 500 price targets.

insights.claim: Despite S&P 500 forward earnings rising about 28% year-to-date, the index itself is up only about 13%, meaning the forward P/E has actually compressed even as earnings surge — a pattern Yardeni frames as fabulous earnings momentum (FIMO) without matching fear-of-missing-out valuation expansion (FOMO).
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A falling multiple alongside surging earnings suggests equities may be under-priced relative to fundamentals rather than in a speculative bubble, an argument for staying invested rather than de-risking on valuation grounds alone.
insights.quote: FIMO fabulous earnings momentum is what's been driving the market higher.

insights.claim: Second-quarter corporate earnings rose about 50% year over year, but roughly half of that reflected mark-to-market gains, leaving underlying growth closer to 25%; analysts still expect greater than 20% earnings growth in both the third and fourth quarters.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Stripping out mark-to-market noise gives a cleaner read on organic earnings growth, which still looks robust enough to support the bull case into year-end.

insights.claim: Analysts' long-term (3-to-5-year) earnings growth expectations are at an all-time record high, implying company earnings growth of over 25% annually — a rate Yardeni calls implausible in an economy currently growing around 6% in nominal terms, suggesting a degree of irrational exuberance on the analyst side even while investors have not bid up valuations to match.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Analyst long-term growth forecasts this extreme are a useful sentiment gauge; a future reset of these expectations toward reality could pressure stocks even if near-term earnings stay solid.

insights.claim: Yardeni's simplified version of the Fed's Stock Valuation Model (which he coined in 1997) says the fair-value P/E equals 1 divided by the 10-year bond yield; with the yield near 5%, that implies a fair-value P/E of about 20, which roughly matches the market's current multiple.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: This gives investors a simple, real-time check on whether the market multiple is stretched relative to bond yields: if yields rise well above 5% without an offsetting P/E cut, equities would screen as overvalued by this model.
insights.quote: 1 divided by five is 20. That's that's the fair value PE

themes.theme: AI and Semiconductors: From Cyclical Fear to Secular Conviction

insights.claim: Meta's announcement of a new AI large language model, and the market's read that it will require significantly more chips, reignited a rally in semiconductors and the Magnificent 7 and shifted sentiment toward treating AI chip demand as a durable secular growth story rather than a boom-bust cyclical one.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A shift from 'cyclical' to 'secular' framing for semiconductors would justify higher sustained multiples for the group, a key debate for anyone sizing AI-infrastructure exposure.

insights.claim: Semiconductor forward P/E multiples have actually declined recently and now trade below the S&P 500's overall multiple, even though semiconductor earnings have gotten 'growthy' — indicating the group is not priced for bubble-like expectations.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A below-market multiple on a sector with strong earnings momentum suggests room for semiconductor stocks to re-rate higher if the secular AI-demand thesis holds.

insights.claim: The combined forward P/E of the information technology and communication services sectors (roughly Meta and Google) has converged to about 19, in line with the broader S&P 500 multiple, in contrast to the dot-com era when those sectors' market-cap share vastly exceeded their earnings share; today the two shares are nearly identical.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Because tech/comm-services market cap is now backed by a matching share of earnings rather than speculative excess, the risk of a dot-com-style melt-up-then-meltdown looks reduced, supporting continued exposure to the group.

insights.claim: Even though technology and communication services screen as cheap relative to earnings, Yardeni is keeping a market-weight (not overweight) stance because the two sectors already make up nearly 50% of the S&P 500 and he doubts they will grow to 65-80% of the index.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Position sizing discipline: valuation cheapness alone isn't a reason to concentrate further in an already-dominant sector weight.

insights.claim: Yardeni argues final demand for AI is effectively unlimited given there is no shortage of usable data, and expects the next wave of demand to come from robotics and humanoid robots, extending the AI capex cycle well beyond current large-language-model applications.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If robotics/humanoid demand becomes a second leg of AI capex, it extends the runway for chip and data-center spending beyond what current LLM-driven forecasts assume.

insights.claim: Yardeni has pushed his S&P 500 target of 8,400 out to the middle of 2026 due to recent PE pressure from Middle East/oil-driven risk, but maintains his longer-term 'Roaring 2020s' thesis targeting S&P 500 10,000 by the end of the decade, and says it could arrive sooner.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The near-term target timeline is more fluid to geopolitical/oil shocks than the multi-year thesis, so investors should treat 8,400 as a soft, revisable checkpoint while the 10,000 decade-end target remains the core long-term call.
insights.quote: bottom line is it's a bull market. Bottom line is still the roaring 2020s. Bottom line is we're still looking for 10,000 by the end of the decade.

insights.claim: A broadening of the market into small- and mid-cap stocks was underway before the recent Middle East escalation, driven by improving earnings in those segments, and Yardeni expects continued broad-based market participation as long as a recession is avoided.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A recession-avoidance call supports staying diversified beyond mega-cap tech rather than concentrating solely in the Magnificent 7 for the next leg of the rally.

themes.theme: Capital Flows, AI Debt Issuance, and the Dollar

insights.claim: Net capital inflows into the United States remain strong overall, but inflows into US Treasuries are slowing while inflows into corporate bonds — including debt issued to finance AI infrastructure — are speeding up, with some of that demand coming from overseas investors.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A rotation of foreign capital from Treasuries into AI-related corporate credit is a flow to monitor for both dollar strength and credit-spread signals in the AI-infrastructure buildout.

insights.claim: Yardeni's long-standing view is that the bond market responds more to inflation expectations and Fed policy than to raw supply and demand, though he acknowledges that record fiscal deficits combined with unprecedented AI-related corporate bond issuance may be making supply/demand dynamics more relevant now than in the past.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: If supply/demand is becoming a bigger driver of yields, investors should watch AI-bond issuance volumes as a new source of upward pressure on long-term rates, not just inflation data.
insights.quote: going where no man and woman has gone before in terms of the size of the deficits

insights.claim: Yardeni's heuristic for a US debt crisis is that he will worry about one only when the bond market itself starts worrying — he flags a 10-year yield spike toward 5.5%-6% as the signal that debt-crisis talk would return, whereas a steady or falling yield near 5% suggests markets remain calm.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete, watchable threshold (10-year yield 5.5%-6%) for when fiscal/debt-crisis narratives should actually be taken seriously versus dismissed as noise.
insights.quote: I'll worry about a debt crisis when the bond market worries about a debt crisis.

insights.claim: Yardeni agrees with an audience observation that persistent negativism from reporters and media commentators about the economy and markets — despite both performing well — has helped keep speculative FOMO buying in check, which he treats as a bullish contrarian signal rather than a warning sign.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Widespread media pessimism amid strong fundamentals is, in Yardeni's framework, a sign that the rally is not yet overheated with speculative excess, arguing against calling a top on sentiment grounds alone.
insights.quote: Never in my experience have I witnessed so much negativism regarding the economy and markets when both have been doing as well as they they are.
